subject: chemistry
title: pH titration curves and indicators
key_idea: A pH curve plots pH against volume of base added. Its shape depends on whether the acid and base are strong or weak. An indicator is suitable when its colour change range lies within the steep part of the curve.

blocks.text: This section covers the four combinations of strong and weak acid with strong and weak base. Each curve is for a monoprotic acid and a monoprotic base.

items.meaning: The point where the acid and base have reacted in exactly the amounts in the equation.
The point where the indicator changes colour.
The steep rise in pH around the equivalence point, from one drop of titrant.

diagram.alt: Two pH curves against volume of base added. The strong acid curve starts low, rises steeply at 25 cm³ and levels at high pH. The weak acid curve starts higher, rises gently, then rises steeply at 25 cm³.

items: A weak acid starts at a higher pH, as it is only partly dissociated.
The equivalence pH is above 7 when the salt formed has a basic anion (weak acid + strong base). It is below 7 when the salt has an acidic cation (strong acid + weak base).
A weak acid + weak base curve has no sharp vertical section, so no indicator is suitable. A pH meter must be used.
Strong acid curves start low. Weak acid curves start higher.
The equivalence pH depends on which of the acid and base is strong.
Weak acid + weak base has no vertical section.

blocks.text: An indicator is itself a weak acid, written HIn. Its two forms have different colours.

blocks.label: An indicator in solution
where: HIn = the acid form, with one colour
In⁻ = the conjugate base form, with a different colour

items: In acid, the added H⁺ shifts the equilibrium left, so the HIn colour shows.
In alkali, OH⁻ removes H⁺, the equilibrium shifts right, and the In⁻ colour shows.
The colour changes over a narrow pH range, where both forms are present.
A suitable indicator changes colour completely within the vertical section of the curve.

options.label: Strong acid + weak base

Choose an indicator whose range falls within the vertical section.

blocks.text: A titration finds an unknown concentration. This section covers the calculation.

items.text: Find moles of the known solution from c × V, with V in dm³.
Use the equation to find moles of the other reactant.
Divide moles by volume in dm³ to find the concentration.

blocks.text: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH needs 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ HCl. n(HCl) = 0.00200 mol, which is 1 : 1, so [NaOH] = 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol/dm³.

items: Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.
Use the balanced equation for the mole ratio.

checks.q: Sketch the pH curve when 0.100 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid is titrated with 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide, and state a suitable indicator.
checks.a: Starts at about pH 3. Rises gradually (buffer region), then a vertical section at the equivalence volume from about pH 7 to 11. Levels off at about pH 13. Phenolphthalein is suitable (changes colour within the vertical section).

checks.q: Explain why methyl orange is not suitable for a weak acid with a strong base.
checks.a: Methyl orange changes colour at pH 3.1 to 4.4, which is before the vertical section; the colour change would happen well before the equivalence point.

checks.q: Explain, using an equilibrium, why an indicator changes colour when alkali is added.
checks.a: HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻. Alkali removes H⁺, so the equilibrium shifts right and the colour of In⁻ shows.

blocks.text: Measuring pH with a pH meter

items: Calibrate the meter with buffer solutions of known pH, such as pH 4, 7 and 10.
Rinse the probe with deionised water between solutions.
Stir the solution and wait for a steady reading before recording the pH.
In a titration, add the titrant in small portions and record pH against volume. Add smaller portions near the vertical section.

blocks.text: Indicator colour in terms of equilibrium
Explain colour changes using HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻. At the end point [HIn] = [In⁻], and the colour is a mix of the two.
A weak acid-strong base curve: buffer action and Ka

items: The gently sloping region before the vertical section is a **buffer region**. The weak acid and its salt are both present, so added OH⁻ changes pH very little.
At half-equivalence, half the weak acid has been neutralised, so [HA] = [A⁻].
Then Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] ÷ [HA] = [H⁺], so pH = pKa at half the equivalence volume.

blocks.text: If the equivalence volume is 25.0 cm³, read the pH at 12.5 cm³ to get pKa.

items: Strong acid + strong base gives about −57 kJ/mol, since the reaction is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
A weak acid gives a less exothermic value, because energy is needed to dissociate the acid as the H⁺ is used up.
